title: Human Research Program Evidence Reports
content:
NASA is preparing for long duration crewed missions beyond low-Earth orbit that will be
challenged in several ways, including long-term exposure to the deep space environment, greater
limitations on resources, no resupply, and increased physical and cognitive demands through
significant expansion of extra-vehicular activities (EVAs). The food system is critical to all aspects
of human health and performance, but it is also the greatest human resource driver on
exploration missions. Currently, no food system has been demonstrated that can meet the
requirements of a long duration exploration mission, making food and nutrition a red risk for
most exploration scenarios, including Mars

title: Human Research Program Evidence Reports
content:
The space food system and the nutrition it delivers is central to health and performance,
and therefore, the success of crewed space exploration missions. If the food system is not safe,
nutritious, and acceptable, then mission objectives or overall mission success may be adversely
affected. The primary goal of the Advanced Food Technology Project (AFT) is to develop
requirements, methods, and technologies that will enable NASA to provide an adequate food
system characterized by the provision of safe, nutritious, and acceptable food to the crew. The
requirements of the food system must be in balance with the requirements of all other systems
and the available vehicle resources such as mass, volume, waste, and crew time

This document presents the evidence for the Risk of Performance Decrement and Crew
Illness Due to an Inadequate Food System and the gaps in relation to exploration, as identified
by the NASA HRP. The research reviewed here indicates strategies that may establish methods,
technologies, and requirements that increase food stability, support adequate nutrition, quality,
and variety, enable supplementation with grow-pick-and-eat salad crops, ensure safety, and
reduce resource use. Obtaining the evidence to establish an adequate food system is essential,
as the resources allocated to the food system may be defined based on the data relating
nutritional stability and food quality requirements to crew performance and health.

title: Human Research Program Evidence Reports
content:
The space food system is unique in that it is a closed, resource limited system that must
provide all nutrition to support high performance in high-stress situations. Throughout history,
food system adequacy has been a critical factor to the success or failure of human exploration.
From 1500-1800, the lack of vitamin C in available rations resulted in rampant scurvy and the
deaths of more sailors than all other causes combined (Pimentel 2003). During early polar
exploration missions, attempts to reduce supply weight by caloric restriction and the dislike of
available foods resulted in significant weight and muscle loss, malnutrition and psychological
distress, which correlated with failed expeditions, and in many cases death (Pugh 1972).
The challenges of food system adequacy in resource limited situations have
commonalities between exploration and military campaigns, and military needs have driven
advances that have been beneficial to both

title: Human Research Program Evidence Reports

s (Heidelbaugh 1966). The space food system has also benefited from commercial food
developments in freeze-drying and other stabilization technologies. However, extended
spaceflight exploration beyond low Earth orbit (LEO) adds new challenges to shelf life, safety, and
resources that will require further advancements.
Processing and packaging ensure a safe and nutritious food system for missions in LEO;
however, nutrition and quality degrade over time under current storage conditions on space
vehicles to a level that will not meet the requirements for a long duration mission. Given that
food is central to every aspect of health and performance, including cognitive and behavioral
outcomes, insufficient nutrition and quality jeopardizes mission success. However, food is also
the greatest human resource requirement for these missions, and factors that support nutrition,
quality, and safety conflict with mission resource constraints

content:
A mission to Mars may be approximately three years in length. The high mass and volume
of a prepackaged food system may require the food to be launched separately and prepositioned
ahead of the crew launch. Towards the end of the mission food may be five years old at the time
of consumption. Currently, NASA’s prepackaged foods have a stated shelf life of about two-to-
three years, far short of the five-year minimum required for Mars missions.
Extensive provisioning strategies must be evaluated to provide a food system that
supports crew health, performance, and well-being within limited resources. These strategies
may include novel processing, packaging, and storage scenarios that support a longer shelf life
for processed foods, and incorporation of bioregenerative foods over time. A food system must
show adequacy in three general areas before consideration for spaceflight

Second, the food system must be shown to maintain or promote the health and performance of

The evidence in this document shows that a closed source, resource-limited food system

exploration has not yet been identified, making food and nutrition a red risk for Mars and some

acceptability is equated to sensory acceptability and includes appearance, flavor, texture, aroma,
and serving temperature. Flight foods are evaluated for sensory acceptability by a panel of 25-
40 untrained consumers. The sensory attributes of the products are rated using a 9.0-point
Hedonic Scale, where 9 is the highest acceptability score (Chambers and Wolf 1996). Food
products must receive an overall score of 6.0 or higher to be considered for inclusion in the space
food system.
Food system variety and usability are also factors used in defining acceptability. A variety
of food is needed to provide the crew choices and to avoid menu fatigue that may result in
reduced consumption, especially in a closed food system where total food quantity may be
limited (Meiselman et al. 2000). Variety and quality are important to motivate consistent caloric
intake and prevent nutritional deficiency and weight loss

B. Acceptability (Palatability, Variety, Usability)
Food has a behavioral and social factor that must be central to development of any space
food system. It is commonly believed that high performers such as astronauts will consume
“anything” to receive their nutrition and accomplish mission goals. In actuality, the contents of
the food system become increasingly important in the harsh environments of isolation and
confinement, where other comforts and familiarities are unavailable (Stuster 1996). Military,
spaceflight, and test data show that if the food is not considered acceptable through the mission,
then body mass and nutritional intake may not be sufficient (Marriott 1995; Sirmons et al. 2020;
Smith et al. 2021).
Food acceptability can be defined and determined in several ways. First, food
acceptability is equated to sensory acceptability and includes appearance, flavor, texture, aroma,
and serving temperature

red including system mass, volume, power, crew time, water use, and waste disposal. The
resources that impact other systems must be quantified as well. For instance, resources required
to ensure food safety of a bioregenerative system, such as cleaning, disinfection, or testing, must
be included in quantification of system resource trades. Additionally, impacts to other systems
and their supplies must be quantified and compatible, such as impacts of a cleaning solution on
the atmosphere and water recycling systems (Douglas et al. 2021b). Ineffective use of vehicle
resources will decrease the possibility of mission success.
Resource constraints on previous space vehicles drove food system requirements and
modifications. The lack of refrigeration required foods to be shelf stable. The production of
byproduct water from fuel cells on the Shuttle supported use of freeze-dried foods that reduced

Finally, food acceptability can be affected by the social context and timing of meals. Food
and mealtimes can play a primary role in psychological-social benefits by promoting unity and
reducing the stress and boredom of prolonged space missions (Stuster 1996).

resources that impact other systems must be quantified as well

D. Stability
Food for spaceflight must maintain both quality and nutrition through the length of the
mission. Exploration missions may require a system to be stable for up to five years, and many
shelf-stable foods do not meet this requirement under ambient storage. Refrigeration for food
storage has not been available on most missions to date due to the high resource need (power,
mass, volume). Bioregenerative food systems may also have components that do not meet the
five-year shelf-life requirement, or which may be sensitive to the radiation levels in deep space.
Potential exposure to high temperatures or significant pressure changes may also impact food
and packaging. For many bioregenerative systems, stability within these constraints is still an
unknown factor.

E. Reliability
Food systems for spaceflight must not be at risk for food scarcity. The prepackaged food
system remains safe as long as packaging remains intact. However, if a bioregenerative system
does not grow as expected or becomes contaminated it could challenge food availability. Due to
this challenge, it is likely that shelf-stable foods will remain an important part of the food system
until formal bioregenerative processes are proven and excess food is available.
F. International Space Station Food System – Current State
The food system used on the International Space Station meets food safety, stability, and
reliability requirements for missions with regular resupply, and efforts are ongoing to improve
choice, acceptability, and food intake to best support health and performance. The current
system consists of processed and prepackaged foods that are tested preflight for safety

Dr. Grace Douglas serves as the lead scientist for NASA’s Advanced Food Technology
research effort, which focuses on determining methods, technologies, and requirements for
developing a safe, nutritious, and palatable food system that will promote astronaut health
during long-duration space missions. Her responsibilities include assessing the risk of an
inadequate food system to crew based on vehicle design and mission concept and developing
the research path that will ensure the food system meets crew health and performance
requirements on spaceflight vehicles.
The author acknowledges the contributions in current and previous Evidence Reports by
various Subject Matter Experts located at Johnson and Kennedy Space Centers and the Food and
Nutrition Risk Custodian team of the Human Safety Risk Board who are responsible for
maintaining the DAG. The author thanks Trent Smith, Matthew Mickens, and Ray Wheeler for
review.
